UNPARALLELED.d: Having no parallel, or equal; unequaled; unmatched. The unparalleled perseverance of the armies of the United States, under every suffering and discouragement, was little short of a miracle. Washington.

m: withered by heat. [Obs.] "My tongue . . . unparched." Crashaw.
UNPARCHED.d: Dried up; withered by heat. [Obs.] "My tongue . . . unparched." Crashaw.

m: Not admitting of pardon or forgiveness
UNPARDONABLE.d: Not admitting of pardon or forgiveness; inexcusable.

m: Having no parent, or no acknowledged parent. [R.]
UNPARENTED.d: Having no parent, or no acknowledged parent. [R.]

m: contrary to the practice of parliamentary bodies. -- Un*par`lia*men"ta*ri*ness, n.
UNPARLIAMENTARY.d: Not parliamentary; contrary to the practice of parliamentary bodies. -- Un*par`lia*men"ta*ri*ness, n.

m: Impartial. [Obs.] Bp. Sanderson. -- Un*par"tial*ly, adv. [Obs.] Hooker.
UNPARTIAL.d: Impartial. [Obs.] Bp. Sanderson. -- Un*par"tial*ly, adv. [Obs.] Hooker.

m: Impassable. E. A. Freeman. -- Un*pass"a*ble*ness, n. Evelyn.
UNPASSABLE.d: Impassable. E. A. Freeman. -- Un*pass"a*ble*ness, n. Evelyn.

m: To cause to be no longer pastor
UNPASTOR.d: To cause to be no longer pastor; to deprive of pastorship. [R.] Fuller.

m: Not paved; not furnished with a pavement. Hakewill.
UNPAVED.d: 1. Not paved; not furnished with a pavement. Hakewill. 2. Castrated. [Obs.] "Unpaved eunuch." Shak.

m: To undo, take back, or annul, as a payment. Shak.
UNPAY.d: To undo, take back, or annul, as a payment. Shak.

m: Absence or lack of peace. [Obs.] Testament of Love.
UNPEACE.d: Absence or lack of peace. [Obs.] Testament of Love.

m: Not distinguished by a pedigree. [R.] Pollok.
UNPEDIGREED.d: Not distinguished by a pedigree. [R.] Pollok.

UNPEERED.d: Having no peer; unequaled; unparalleled. "Unpeered excellence." Marston.

m: To remove a peg or pegs from
UNPEG.d: To remove a peg or pegs from; to unfasten; to open. Shak.

UNPERSUASION.d: The state of not being persuaded; disbelief; doubt. [R.] Abp. Leighton.

picked open. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + picked.] Not picked. Milton.

UNPITIOUS.d: 1. Impious; wicked. [Obs.] "The life of the unpitous." Wyclif (Prov. xv. 8). 2. Destitute of pity; pitiless. [Obs.] Chaucer. -- Un*pi"tous*ly, adv. [Obs.] -- Un*pi"tous*ness, n. [Obs.] Wyclif.

UNPLAINED.d: Not deplored or bewailed; unlamented. [Obs.] Spenser.

UNPLAT.d: To take out the folds or twists of, as something previously platted; to unfold; to unwreathe.

m: To deprive of lead, as of a leaden coffin. [R.] Burke.
UNPLUMB.d: To deprive of lead, as of a leaden coffin. [R.] Burke.

UNPLUME.d: To strip of plumes or feathers; hence, to humiliate.

UNPOISED.d: 1. Not poised or balanced. 2. Not poised or weighed; hence, regardless of consequences; unhesitating. [Obs.] Marston.

m: To remove or expel poison from. [Obs.] South.
UNPOISON.d: To remove or expel poison from. [Obs.] South.

UNPOLICIED.d: 1. Not having civil polity, or a regular form of government. 2. Impolitic; imprudent. [Obs.] Shak.

m: To revoke or annul by prayer, as something previously prayed for. [R.] Sir M. Hale.
UNPRAY.d: To revoke or annul by prayer, as something previously prayed for. [R.] Sir M. Hale.

m: Not to be influenced or moved by prayers
UNPRAYABLE.d: Not to be influenced or moved by prayers; obdurate. [R.] Wyclif.

m: Not prayed for. [Obs.] Sir T. More.
UNPRAYED.d: Not prayed for. [Obs.] Sir T. More.

m: To undo or overthrow by preaching. [R.] De Foe.
UNPREACH.d: To undo or overthrow by preaching. [R.] De Foe.

m: not preceded by a like case

UNPRECEDENTED.d: Having no precedent or example; not preceded by a like case; not having the authority of prior example; novel; new; unexampled. -- Un*prec"e*dent*ed*ly, adv.

m: To retract or falsify a previous prediction. Milton.
UNPREDICT.d: To retract or falsify a previous prediction. Milton.

also, priceless. "Amethyst unpriced." Neale (Rhythm of St. Bernard).

m: To deprive of the character or authority of a prince

m: To destroy the moral principles of. [R.]

m: especially, being without right moral principles

UNPRISON.d: To take or deliver from prison.

UNPRIZABLE.d: 1. Not prized or valued; being without value. [Obs.] 2. Invaluable; being beyond estimation. [Obs.]

m: Want of proficiency or improvement. Bp. Hall.
UNPROFICIENCY.d: Want of proficiency or improvement. Bp. Hall.

m: To revoke or annul, as a promise. Chapman.
UNPROMISE.d: To revoke or annul, as a promise. Chapman.

m: To remove a prop or props from
UNPROP.d: To remove a prop or props from; to deprive of support.

UNPROVIDE.d: To deprive of necessary provision; to unfurnish. Lest her . . . beauty unprovide my mind again. Shak.

m: Improvident. [Obs.] "Who for thyself art so unprovident.' Shak.
UNPROVIDENT.d: Improvident. [Obs.] "Who for thyself art so unprovident.' Shak.

m: Imprudent. [Obs.] "The most unwise and unprudential act." Milton.
UNPRUDENTIAL.d: Imprudent. [Obs.] "The most unwise and unprudential act." Milton.

m: To smooth away the puckers or wrinkles of.

m: Deprived of the usual faculties. [Obs.] Shak.
UNQUALITIED.d: Deprived of the usual faculties. [Obs.] Shak.

m: to idealize. His fancy . . . unrealizes everything at a touch. Lowell.
UNREALIZE.d: To make unreal; to idealize. His fancy . . . unrealizes everything at a touch. Lowell.

m: absurdity. Abbot of Unreason. See Abbot of Misrule, under Abbot. To undo, disprove, or refute by reasoning. [Obs.] To unreason the equity of God's proceedings. South.
UNREASON.d: Want of reason; unreasonableness; absurdity. Abbot of Unreason. See Abbot of Misrule, under Abbot.  To undo, disprove, or refute by reasoning. [Obs.] To unreason the equity of God's proceedings. South.

UNREASONABLE.d: Not reasonable; irrational; immoderate; exorbitant. -- Un*rea"son*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*rea"son*a*bly, adv.

UNREASONED.d: Not supported by reason; unreasonable. "Unreasoned habits." Burke.

UNREAVE.d: To unwind; to disentangle; to loose. [Obs.] Spenser.

m: not torn to pieces. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
UNREAVED.d: Not torn, split, or parted; not torn to pieces. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

UNREBUKABLE.d: Not deserving rebuke or censure; blameless. 1 Tim. vi. 14.

m: To withdraw, or take out, as a rope from a block, thimble, or the like.
UNREEVE.d: To withdraw, or take out, as a rope from a block, thimble, or the like.

m: state of being unreformed. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
UNREFORMATION.d: Want of reformation; state of being unreformed. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

m: The quality or state of being unregenerate. Glanvill.
UNREGENERACY.d: The quality or state of being unregenerate. Glanvill.

m: remaining or being at enmity with God.
UNREGENERATE.d: Not regenerated; not renewed in heart; remaining or being at enmity with God.

m: remaining or being at enmity with God.
UNREGENERATED.d: Not regenerated; not renewed in heart; remaining or being at enmity with God.

UNREIN.d: To loosen the reins of; to remove restraint from. Addison.

UNRELENTING.d: Not relenting; unyielding; rigid; hard; stern; cruel. -- Un`re*lent"ing*ly, adv. -- Un`re*lent"ing*ness, n.

m: untrustworthy. See Reliable. -- Un`re*li"a*ble*ness, n. Alcibiades . . . was too unsteady, and (according to Mr. Coleridge's coinage) "unreliable;" or perhaps, in more correct English, too "unrelyuponable." De Quincey.
UNRELIABLE.d: Not reliable; untrustworthy. See Reliable. -- Un`re*li"a*ble*ness, n. Alcibiades . . . was too unsteady, and (according to Mr. Coleridge's coinage) "unreliable;" or perhaps, in more correct English, too "unrelyuponable." De Quincey.

UNREMEMBRANCE.d: Want of remembrance; forgetfulness. I. Watts.

UNREMITTING.d: Not remitting; incessant; continued; persevering; as, unremitting exertions. Cowper. -- Un`re*mit"ting*ly, adv. -- Un`re*mit"ting*ness, n.

m: Not capable of being reprieved. Shak.
UNREPRIEVABLE.d: Not capable of being reprieved. Shak.

UNREPROACHABLE.d: Not liable to be reproached; irreproachable.

m: Not having incurred reproof, blameless. [Obs.] In unreproved pleasures free. Milton.
UNREPROVED.d: 1. Not reproved. Sandys. 2. Not having incurred reproof, blameless. [Obs.] In unreproved pleasures free. Milton.

UNRESERVE.d: Absence of reverse; frankness; freedom of communication. T. Warton.

UNRESERVED.d: Not reserved; not kept back; not withheld in part; unrestrained. -- Un`re*serv"ed*ly, adv. -- Un`re*serv"ed*ness, n.

UNRESISTANCE.d: Nonresistance; passive submission; irresistance. Bp. Hall.

UNRESISTED.d: 1. Not resisted; unopposed. Bentley. 2. Resistless; as, unresisted fate. [R.] Pope.

m: Disrespect. [Obs.] "Unrespect of her toil." Bp. Hall.
UNRESPECT.d: Disrespect. [Obs.] "Unrespect of her toil." Bp. Hall.

UNREST.d: Want of rest or repose; unquietness; sleeplessness; uneasiness; disquietude. Is this, quoth she, the cause of your unrest! Chaucer. Can calm despair and wild unrest Be tenants of a single breast Tennyson.

UNRESTRAINT.d: Freedom from restraint; freedom; liberty; license.

UNRESTY.d: Causing unrest; disquieting; as, unresty sorrows. [Obs.] Chaucer.

m: Not furnished with a revenue. [R.] Milton.
UNREVENUED.d: Not furnished with a revenue. [R.] Milton.

UNREVERENCE.d: Absence or lack of reverence; irreverence. [Obs.] Wyclif.

m: as, to unriddle an enigma or a mystery. Macaulay. And where you can't unriddle, learn to trust. Parnell.
UNRIDDLE.d: To read the riddle of; to solve or explain; as, to unriddle an enigma or a mystery. Macaulay. And where you can't unriddle, learn to trust. Parnell.

m: as, to unrig a ship. Totten.
UNRIG.d: To strip of rigging; as, to unrig a ship. Totten.

m: wrong. [Obs.] Gower. A wrong. [Obs.] Nor did I you never unright. Chaucer. To cause (something right) to become wrong. [Obs.] Gower.
UNRIGHT.d: Not right; wrong. [Obs.] Gower.  A wrong. [Obs.] Nor did I you never unright. Chaucer.  To cause (something right) to become wrong. [Obs.] Gower.

m: Contrary to law and equity; unjust -- Un*right"eous*ly, adv. -- Un*right"eous*ness, n.
UNRIGHTEOUS.d: 1. Not righteous; evil; wicked; sinful; as, an unrighteous man. 2. Contrary to law and equity; unjust; as, an unrighteous decree or sentence. -- Un*right"eous*ly, adv. -- Un*right"eous*ness, n.

m: Not having a ring, as in the nose. "Pigs unringed." Hudibras.
UNRINGED.d: Not having a ring, as in the nose. "Pigs unringed." Hudibras.

m: Free from rioting. [Obs.] "A chaste, unrioted house." May (Lucan).
UNRIOTED.d: Free from rioting. [Obs.] "A chaste, unrioted house." May (Lucan).

UNRIP.d: To rip; to cut open. Bacon.

m: Developing too early; premature. Sir P. Sidney.
as, unripe fruit. 2. Developing too early
UNRIPE.d: 1. Not ripe; as, unripe fruit. 2. Developing too early; premature. Sir P. Sidney.

m: Quality or state of being unripe.
UNRIPENESS.d: Quality or state of being unripe.

UNRIVALED.d: Having no rival; without a competitor; peerless. [Spelt also unrivalled.] Pope.

m: To take out, or loose, the rivets of
UNRIVET.d: To take out, or loose, the rivets of; as, to unrivet boiler plates.

UNROBE.d: To disrobe; to undress; to take off the robes.

m: To open, as what is rolled or convolved to unroll a banner.
To remove from a roll or register, as a name. If I make not this cheat bring out another . . . let me be unrolled and my name put in the book of virtue! Shak.
UNROLL.d: 1. To open, as what is rolled or convolved; as, to unroll cloth; to unroll a banner. 2. To display; to reveal. Dryden. 3. To remove from a roll or register, as a name. If I make not this cheat bring out another . . . let me be unrolled and my name put in the book of virtue! Shak.

m: To strip off the roof or covering of, as a house. Shak.
UNROOF.d: To strip off the roof or covering of, as a house. Shak.

m: Etym: [Properly p. p. of unroof.] Stripped of a roof, or similar covering. Broken carriages, dead horses, unroofed cottages, all indicated the movements. Sir W. Scott.
Etym: [Pref. un- not + roofed.] Not yet roofed.
UNROOFED.d: 1. Etym: [Properly p. p. of unroof.]  Stripped of a roof, or similar covering. Broken carriages, dead horses, unroofed cottages, all indicated the movements. Sir W. Scott. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + roofed.]  Not yet roofed.

m: To drive from the roost. Shak.
UNROOST.d: To drive from the roost. Shak.

m: To tear up by the roots
to uproot. To be torn up by the roots. Beau. & Fl.
UNROOT.d: To tear up by the roots; to eradicate; to uproot.  To be torn up by the roots. Beau. & Fl.

m: Excessively rude. [Obs. & R.] "See how the unrude rascal backbites him." B. Jonson.
e: See how the unrude rascal backbites him.
UNRUDE.d: 1. Not rude; polished. Herrick. 2. Excessively rude. [Obs. & R.] "See how the unrude rascal backbites him." B. Jonson.

m: To cease from being ruffled or agitated. Dryden.
UNRUFFLE.d: To cease from being ruffled or agitated. Dryden.

m: quiet. Calm and unruffled as a summer's sea. Addison.
UNRUFFLED.d: Not ruffled or agitated; smooth; calm; tranquil; quiet. Calm and unruffled as a summer's sea. Addison.

m: Not ruined or destroyed. [Obs.] "Unruinated towers." Bp. Hall.
UNRUINATE.d: Not ruined or destroyed. [Obs.] "Unruinated towers." Bp. Hall.

m: Not ruined or destroyed. [Obs.] "Unruinated towers." Bp. Hall.
UNRUINATED.d: Not ruined or destroyed. [Obs.] "Unruinated towers." Bp. Hall.

m: Not governed or controlled. "Unruled and undirected." Spenser.
Not ruled or marked with lines
UNRULED.d: 1. Not governed or controlled. "Unruled and undirected." Spenser. 2. Not ruled or marked with lines; as, unruled paper.

m: Unruliness. [Obs.] "Breaking forth with rude unruliment." Spenser.
UNRULIMENT.d: Unruliness. [Obs.] "Breaking forth with rude unruliment." Spenser.

UNRULY.d: Not submissive to rule; disregarding restraint; disposed to violate; turbulent; ungovernable; refractory; as, an unruly boy; unruly boy; unruly conduct. But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison. James iii. 8.

UNRUMPLE.d: To free from rumples; to spread or lay even,

m: To deprive of sacramental character or efficacy
as, to unsacrament the rite of baptism. [Obs.]
UNSACRAMENT.d: To deprive of sacramental character or efficacy; as, to unsacrament the rite of baptism. [Obs.]

m: fickle. [Obs.] O, stormy people, unsad and ever untrue. Chaucer.
UNSAD.d: Unsteady; fickle. [Obs.] O, stormy people, unsad and ever untrue. Chaucer.

UNSADDEN.d: To relieve from sadness; to cheer. [R.] Whitlock.

m: To strip of a saddle; to take the saddle from, as a horse.
To throw from the saddle; to unhorse.
UNSADDLE.d: 1. To strip of a saddle; to take the saddle from, as a horse. 2. To throw from the saddle; to unhorse.

m: The quality or state of being in peril
UNSAFETY.d: The quality or state of being in peril; absence of safety; insecurity. Bacon.

UNSAINT.d: To deprive of saintship; to deny sanctity to. [R.] South.

m: unmerchantable. -- n. That which can not be sold. Byron.
UNSALABLE.d: Not salable; unmerchantable. -- n.  That which can not be sold. Byron.

m: Absence or lack of sanctification. Shak.
UNSANCTIFICATION.d: Absence or lack of sanctification. Shak.

m: Insatiable. [Obs.] Hooker. -- Un*sa"ti*a*ble*ness, n. [Obs.] -- Un*sa"ti*a*bly, adv. [Obs.]
UNSATIABLE.d: Insatiable. [Obs.] Hooker. -- Un*sa"ti*a*ble*ness, n. [Obs.] -- Un*sa"ti*a*bly, adv. [Obs.]

m: Capable of absorbing or dissolving to a greater degree
(Chem.) Capable of taking up, or of uniting with, certain other elements or compounds, without the elimination of any side product; thus, aldehyde, ethylene, and ammonia are unsaturated.
UNSATURATED.d: 1. Capable of absorbing or dissolving to a greater degree; as, an unsaturated solution. 2. (Chem.)  Capable of taking up, or of uniting with, certain other elements or compounds, without the elimination of any side product; thus, aldehyde, ethylene, and ammonia are unsaturated.

m: The quality or state of being unsaturated.
UNSATURATION.d: The quality or state of being unsaturated.

m: To recant or recall, as what has been said
to make as if not said. You can say and unsay things at pleasure. Goldsmith.
UNSAY.d: To recant or recall, as what has been said; to refract; to take back again; to make as if not said. You can say and unsay things at pleasure. Goldsmith.

m: to remove scales from. [An eagle] purging and unscaling her long-abused sight at the fountain itself of heavenly radiance. Milton.
UNSCALE.d: To divest of scales; to remove scales from. [An eagle] purging and unscaling her long-abused sight at the fountain itself of heavenly radiance. Milton.

m: Etym: [Pref. un- not + sceptered.] Having no scepter.
Etym: [1st pref. un- + scepter.] Deprived of a scepter.
UNSCEPTERED.d: 1. Etym: [Pref. un- not + sceptered.]  Having no scepter. 2. Etym: [1st pref. un- + scepter.]  Deprived of a scepter.

m: Etym: [Pref. un- not + sceptered.] Having no scepter.
Etym: [1st pref. un- + scepter.] Deprived of a scepter.
UNSCEPTRED.d: 1. Etym: [Pref. un- not + sceptered.]  Having no scepter. 2. Etym: [1st pref. un- + scepter.]  Deprived of a scepter.

m: ignorance. [Obs.] If that any wight ween a thing to be otherwise than it is, it is not only unscience, but it is deceivable opinion. Chaucer.
UNSCIENCE.d: Want of science or knowledge; ignorance. [Obs.] If that any wight ween a thing to be otherwise than it is, it is not only unscience, but it is deceivable opinion. Chaucer.

m: to loosen or withdraw (anything, as a screw) by turning it.
UNSCREW.d: To draw the screws from; to loose from screws; to loosen or withdraw (anything, as a screw) by turning it.

UNSCRUPULOUS.d: Not scrupulous; unprincipled. -- Un*scru"pu*lous*ly, adv. -- Un*scru"pu*lous*ness, n.

m: To break or remove the seal of; to open, as what is sealed Unable to unseal his lips beyond the width of a quarter of an inch. Sir W. Scott.
To disclose, as a secret. [Obs.] The Coronation.
UNSEAL.d: 1. To break or remove the seal of; to open, as what is sealed; as, to unseal a letter. Unable to unseal his lips beyond the width of a quarter of an inch. Sir W. Scott. 2. To disclose, as a secret. [Obs.] The Coronation.

m: To open the seam or seams of
UNSEAM.d: To open the seam or seams of; to rip; to cut; to cut open. Shak.

m: mysterious. The counsels of God are to us unsearchable. Rogers. -- Un*search"a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*search"a*bly, adv.
UNSEARCHABLE.d: Not searchable; inscrutable; hidden; mysterious. The counsels of God are to us unsearchable. Rogers. -- Un*search"a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*search"a*bly, adv.

m: To make unseasoned; to deprive of seasoning.
To strike unseasonably; to affect disagreeably or unfavorably. [Obs.] Why do I send this rustic madrigal, That may thy tuneful ear unseason quite Spenser.
UNSEASON.d: 1. To make unseasoned; to deprive of seasoning. 2. To strike unseasonably; to affect disagreeably or unfavorably. [Obs.] Why do I send this rustic madrigal, That may thy tuneful ear unseason quite Spenser.

m: being, done, or occurring out of the proper season
UNSEASONABLE.d: Not seasonable; being, done, or occurring out of the proper season; ill-timed; untimely; too early or too late; as, he called at an unseasonable hour; unseasonable advice; unseasonable frosts; unseasonable food. -- Un*sea"son*a*ble*ness, n. -- Un*sea"son*a*bly, adv.

m: To throw from one's seat; to deprive of a seat. Cowper.
Specifically, to deprive of the right to sit in a legislative body, as for fraud in election. Macaulay.
UNSEAT.d: 1. To throw from one's seat; to deprive of a seat. Cowper. 2. Specifically, to deprive of the right to sit in a legislative body, as for fraud in election. Macaulay.

m: Not seconded; not supported, aided, or assisted the attempt was unseconded.
Not exemplified a second time. [Obs.] "Strange and unseconded shapes of worms." Sir T. Browne.
e: Strange and unseconded shapes of worms.
UNSECONDED.d: 1. Not seconded; not supported, aided, or assisted; as, the motion was unseconded; the attempt was unseconded. 2. Not exemplified a second time. [Obs.] "Strange and unseconded shapes of worms." Sir T. Browne.

UNSECRET.d: To disclose; to divulge. [Obs.] Bacon.  Not secret; not close; not trusty; indiscreet. [Obs.] "We are unsecret to ourselves." Shak.

m: To cause to become not secular
UNSECULARIZE.d: To cause to become not secular; to detach from secular things; to alienate from the world.

m: To open, as the eyes of a hawk that have been seeled
UNSEEL.d: To open, as the eyes of a hawk that have been seeled; hence, to give light to; to enlighten. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

m: The quality or state of being unseemly
UNSEEMLINESS.d: The quality or state of being unseemly; unbecomingness. Udall.

m: indecent. An unseemly outbreak of temper. Hawthorne. In an unseemly manner.
UNSEEMLY.d: Not seemly; unbecoming; indecent. An unseemly outbreak of temper. Hawthorne.  In an unseemly manner.

UNSEEN.d: 1. Not seen or discovered. 2. Unskilled; inexperienced. [Obs.] Clarendon.

m: unfortunate. [Written also unsilly.] [Obs.] Chaucer. -- Un*se"li*ness, n. [Obs.] Chaucer.
UNSELY.d: Not blessed or happy; wretched; unfortunate. [Written also unsilly.] [Obs.] Chaucer. -- Un*se"li*ness, n. [Obs.] Chaucer.

m: Deprived of virility, or seminal energy
UNSEMINARED.d: Deprived of virility, or seminal energy; made a eunuch. [Obs.]

UNSENSED.d: Wanting a distinct meaning; having no certain signification. [R.] Puller.

m: To elevate from the domain of the senses
UNSENSUALIZE.d: To elevate from the domain of the senses; to purify. Coleridge.

UNSERVICE.d: Neglect of duty; idleness; indolence. [Obs.] Massinger.

UNSET.d: Not set; not fixed or appointed.

m: To move or loosen from a settled position or state
to confuse. To become unsettled or unfixed
UNSETTLE.d: To move or loosen from a settled position or state; to unfix; to displace; to disorder; to confuse.  To become unsettled or unfixed; to be disordered. Shak.

m: The quality or state of being unsettled.
UNSETTLEDNESS.d: The quality or state of being unsettled.

m: The act of unsettling, or state of being unsettled
UNSETTLEMENT.d: The act of unsettling, or state of being unsettled; disturbance. J. H. Newman.

m: to make to be no longer seven. [Obs. & R.] "To unseven the sacraments of the church of Rome." Fuller.
UNSEVEN.d: To render other than seven; to make to be no longer seven. [Obs. & R.] "To unseven the sacraments of the church of Rome." Fuller.

m: To undo, as something sewn, or something inclosed by sewing
to take out the stitches of.
UNSEW.d: To undo, as something sewn, or something inclosed by sewing; to rip apart; to take out the stitches of.

m: To deprive of sex, or of qualities becoming to one's sex
esp., to make unfeminine in character, manners, duties, or the like
UNSEX.d: To deprive of sex, or of qualities becoming to one's sex; esp., to make unfeminine in character, manners, duties, or the like; as, to unsex a woman.

m: not proper or peculiar to one of the sexes. De Quincey.
UNSEXUAL.d: Not sexual; not proper or peculiar to one of the sexes. De Quincey.

m: To loose from shackles or bonds
UNSHACKLE.d: To loose from shackles or bonds; to set free from restraint; to unfetter. Addison.

UNSHAKABLE.d: Not capable of being shaken; firm; fixed. Shak. J. S. Mill.

m: To strip the shale, or husk, from
to uncover. [Obs.] I will not unshale the jest before it be ripe. Marston.
UNSHALE.d: To strip the shale, or husk, from; to uncover. [Obs.] I will not unshale the jest before it be ripe. Marston.

m: To deprive of shape, or of proper shape
UNSHAPE.d: To deprive of shape, or of proper shape; to disorder; to confound; to derange. [R.] Shak.

UNSHAPED.d: Not shaped; shapeless; misshapen; deformed; ugly.

UNSHAPEN.d: Not shaped; shapeless; misshapen; deformed; ugly.

m: to draw from the sheath or scabbard, as a sword. To unsheathe the sword, to make war.
UNSHEATHE.d: To deprive of a sheath; to draw from the sheath or scabbard, as a sword. To unsheathe the sword, to make war.

m: Not parted or divided, as the hair. [Obs.] Spenser.
Not spilt, or made to flow, as blood or tears. Milton.
UNSHED.d: 1. Not parted or divided, as the hair. [Obs.] Spenser. 2. Not spilt, or made to flow, as blood or tears. Milton.

m: to take out of the shell
UNSHELL.d: To strip the shell from; to take out of the shell; to hatch.

m: To remove from, or as from, a shelf.
UNSHELVE.d: To remove from, or as from, a shelf.

UNSHENT.d: Not shent; not disgraced; blameless. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

m: To depose from the office of sheriff. [R.]
UNSHERIFF.d: To depose from the office of sheriff. [R.]

m: To take out of a ship or vessel
(Naut.) To remove or detach, as any part or implement, from its proper position or connection when in use to unship capstan bars; to unship the tiller.
UNSHIP.d: 1. To take out of a ship or vessel; as, to unship goods. 2. (Naut.)  To remove or detach, as any part or implement, from its proper position or connection when in use; as, to unship an oar; to unship capstan bars; to unship the tiller.

m: The act of unshipping, or the state of being unshipped
UNSHIPMENT.d: The act of unshipping, or the state of being unshipped; displacement.

m: To remove the shot from, as from a shotted gun
to unload. Not hit by a shot
also, not discharged or fired off.
UNSHOT.d: To remove the shot from, as from a shotted gun; to unload.  Not hit by a shot; also, not discharged or fired off.

m: To recall what is done by shouting. [Obs.] Shak.
UNSHOUT.d: To recall what is done by shouting. [Obs.] Shak.

UNSHROUD.d: To remove the shroud from; to uncover. P. Fletcher.

m: To open, or throw open. [Obs.] Chaucer.
UNSHUT.d: To open, or throw open. [Obs.] Chaucer.

m: To open or remove the shutters of. T. Hughes.
UNSHUTTER.d: To open or remove the shutters of. T. Hughes.

m: not seeing or examining. [Colloq.] Unsight unseen, a colloquial phrase, denoting unseeing unseen, or unseen repeated

as, to buy a thing unsight unseen, that is, without seeing it. For to subscribe, unsight, unseen, To a new church discipline. Hudibras. There was a great confluence of chapmen, that resorted from every part, with a design to purchase, which they were to do "unsight unseen." Spectator.
UNSIGHT.d: Doing or done without sight; not seeing or examining. [Colloq.] Unsight unseen, a colloquial phrase, denoting unseeing unseen, or unseen repeated; as, to buy a thing unsight unseen, that is, without seeing it. For to subscribe, unsight, unseen, To a new church discipline. Hudibras. There was a great confluence of chapmen, that resorted from every part, with a design to purchase, which they were to do "unsight unseen." Spectator.

m: (Gun.) Not aimed by means of a sight; also, not furnished with a sight, or with a properly adjusted sight
e: to shoot and unsighted rife or cannon
UNSIGHTED.d: 1. Not sighted, or seen. Suckling. 2. (Gun.)  Not aimed by means of a sight; also, not furnished with a sight, or with a properly adjusted sight; as, to shoot and unsighted rife or cannon.

UNSIMPLICITY.d: Absence of simplicity; artfulness. C. Kingsley.

m: To deprive of sinfulness, as a sin
UNSIN.d: To deprive of sinfulness, as a sin; to make sinless. [Obs.] Feltham.

UNSINCERE.d: Not sincere or pure; insincere. [Obs.] Dryden. -- Un`sin*cere"ness, n. [Obs.]

m: The quality or state of being unsincere or impure
UNSINCERITY.d: The quality or state of being unsincere or impure; insincerity. [Obs.] Boyle.

m: To deprive of sinews or of strength. [R.] Dryden.
UNSINEW.d: To deprive of sinews or of strength. [R.] Dryden.

UNSISTER.d: To separate, as sisters; to disjoin. [Poetic & R.] Tennyson.

UNSITTING.d: Not sitting well; unbecoming. [Obs.] "Unsitting words." Sir T. More.

UNSKILL.d: Want of skill; ignorance; unskillfulness. [Obs.] Sylvester.

m: Not skillful; inexperienced; awkward; bungling an unskillful logician.
Lacking discernment; injudicious; ignorant. Though it make the unskillful laugh, can not but make the judicious grieve. Shak. -- Un*skill"ful*ly, adv. -- Un*skill"ful*ness, n.
UNSKILLFUL.d: 1. Not skillful; inexperienced; awkward; bungling; as, an unskillful surgeon or mechanic; an unskillful logician. 2. Lacking discernment; injudicious; ignorant. Though it make the unskillful laugh, can not but make the judicious grieve. Shak. -- Un*skill"ful*ly, adv. -- Un*skill"ful*ness, n.

UNSLACKED.d: Not slacked; unslaked; as, unslacked lime.

UNSLAKED.d: Not slaked; unslacked; as, an unslaked thirst; unslaked lime.

m: To take off the slings of, as a yard, a cask, or the like
to release from the slings. Totten.
UNSLING.d: To take off the slings of, as a yard, a cask, or the like; to release from the slings. Totten.

m: to open the sluice or sluices of
UNSLUICE.d: To sluice; to open the sluice or sluices of; to let flow; to discharge. Dryden.

m: The quality or state of being unsociable
UNSOCIABILITY.d: The quality or state of being unsociable; unsociableness.

m: as, an unsociable person or temper. -- Un*so"cia*ble*ness, n. -- Un*so"cia*bly, adv.
UNSOCIABLE.d: Not sociable; not inclined to society; averse to companionship or conversation; solitary; reserved; as, an unsociable person or temper. -- Un*so"cia*ble*ness, n. -- Un*so"cia*bly, adv.

m: To loose or take from a socket.
UNSOCKET.d: To loose or take from a socket.

m: rough. [Obs.] "Bristles of his beard unsoft." Chaucer. Not softly. [Obs.] Great climbers fall unsoft. Spenser.
UNSOFT.d: Not soft; hard; coarse; rough. [Obs.] "Bristles of his beard unsoft." Chaucer.  Not softly. [Obs.] Great climbers fall unsoft. Spenser.

m: To separate or disunite, as what has been soldered
to sunder. [Formerly written also unsoder.] Tennyson.
UNSOLDER.d: To separate or disunite, as what has been soldered; hence, to divide; to sunder. [Formerly written also unsoder.] Tennyson.

UNSOLDIERED.d: Not equipped like a soldier; unsoldierlike. [Obs.] J. Fletcher.

UNSOPHISTICATE.d: Not sophisticated; pure; innocent; genuine. -- Un`so*phis"ti*ca`ted*ness, n.

UNSOPHISTICATED.d: Not sophisticated; pure; innocent; genuine. -- Un`so*phis"ti*ca`ted*ness, n.

UNSORROWED.d: Not sorrowed for; unlamented. Beau. & Fl.

m: Not well selected; ill-chosen. The purpose you undertake is dangerous; the friends you named uncertain; the time itself unsorted. Shak.
UNSORTED.d: 1. Not sorted; not classified; as, a lot of unsorted goods. 2. Not well selected; ill-chosen. The purpose you undertake is dangerous; the friends you named uncertain; the time itself unsorted. Shak.

m: To deprive of soul, spirit, or principle. [R.] Shelton.
UNSOUL.d: To deprive of soul, spirit, or principle. [R.] Shelton.

UNSOUND.d: Not sound; not whole; not solid; defective; infirm; diseased. -- Un*sound"ly, adv. -- Un*sound"ness, n.

m: To take the spars, stakes, or bars from. [R.] Sir W. Scott.
UNSPAR.d: To take the spars, stakes, or bars from. [R.] Sir W. Scott.

m: Not sparing; not parsimonious; liberal; profuse. Burke.
Not merciful or forgiving. [R.] Milton. -- Un*spar"ing*ly, adv. -- Un*spar"ing*ness, n.
UNSPARING.d: 1. Not sparing; not parsimonious; liberal; profuse. Burke. 2. Not merciful or forgiving. [R.] Milton. -- Un*spar"ing*ly, adv. -- Un*spar"ing*ness, n.

m: To retract, as what has been spoken
UNSPEAK.d: To retract, as what has been spoken; to recant; to unsay. [R.] Shak.

m: incapable of being uttered or adequately described
UNSPEAKABLE.d: Not speakable; incapable of being uttered or adequately described; inexpressible; unutterable; ineffable; as, unspeakable grief or rage. -- Un*speak"a*bly, adv. Ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. 1 Pet. i. 8.

m: specifically (Biol.), not adapted, or set apart, for any particular purpose or function
as, an unspecialized unicellular organism. W. K. Brooks.
UNSPECIALIZED.d: Not specialized; specifically (Biol.), not adapted, or set apart, for any particular purpose or function; as, an unspecialized unicellular organism. W. K. Brooks.

m: To break the power of (a spell)
to release (a person) from the influence of a spell
to disenchant. [R.] Such practices as these, . . . The more judicious Israelites unspelled. Dryden.
UNSPELL.d: To break the power of (a spell); to release (a person) from the influence of a spell; to disenchant. [R.] Such practices as these, . . . The more judicious Israelites unspelled. Dryden.

m: To remove, as a planet, from its sphere or orb. Shak.
UNSPHERE.d: To remove, as a planet, from its sphere or orb. Shak.

m: To remove a spike from, as from the vent of a cannon.
UNSPIKE.d: To remove a spike from, as from the vent of a cannon.

UNSPILT.d: Not spilt or wasted; not shed.

UNSPOTTED.d: Not spotted; free from spot or stain; especially, free from moral stain; unblemished; immaculate; as, an unspotted reputation. -- Un*spot"ted*ness, n.

m: To divest of the title or privilege of an esquire. Swift.
UNSQUIRE.d: To divest of the title or privilege of an esquire. Swift.

m: subject to change or overthrow. -- Un*sta"ble*ness, n. Chaucer. Unstable equilibrium. See Stable equilibrium, under Stable.
UNSTABLE.d: Not stable; not firm, fixed, or constant; subject to change or overthrow. -- Un*sta"ble*ness, n. Chaucer. Unstable equilibrium. See Stable equilibrium, under Stable.

m: To remove, or take away, from a stack
to remove, as something constituting a stack.
UNSTACK.d: To remove, or take away, from a stack; to remove, as something constituting a stack.

UNSTARCH.d: To free from starch; to make limp or pliable.

m: To deprive of state or dignity. [R.] High-battled Cæsar will unstate his happiness. Shak.
UNSTATE.d: To deprive of state or dignity. [R.] High-battled Cæsar will unstate his happiness. Shak.

m: To remove, as a mast, from its step.
UNSTEP.d: To remove, as a mast, from its step.

m: To release, as one thing stuck to another. Richardson.
UNSTICK.d: To release, as one thing stuck to another. Richardson.

m: to remove the sting of. [R.] "Elegant dissertations on virtue and vice . . . will not unsting calamity." J. M. Mason.
UNSTING.d: To disarm of a sting; to remove the sting of. [R.] "Elegant dissertations on virtue and vice . . . will not unsting calamity." J. M. Mason.

m: To open by picking out stitches
to take out, or undo, the stitches of
as, to unstitch a seam. Collier.
UNSTITCH.d: To open by picking out stitches; to take out, or undo, the stitches of; as, to unstitch a seam. Collier.

m: To deprive of a stock; to remove the stock from; to loose from that which fixes, or holds fast.
To remove from the stocks, as a ship.
UNSTOCK.d: 1. To deprive of a stock; to remove the stock from; to loose from that which fixes, or holds fast. 2. To remove from the stocks, as a ship.

m: Etym: [Pref. un- not + stocking.] Destitute of stockings. Sir W. Scott.
Etym: [1st pref. un- + stocking.] Deprived of stockings.
UNSTOCKINGED.d: 1. Etym: [Pref. un- not + stocking.]  Destitute of stockings. Sir W. Scott. 2. Etym: [1st pref. un- + stocking.]  Deprived of stockings.

m: To take the stopple or stopper from
To free from any obstruction; to open.
e: to unstop a bottle or a cask
UNSTOP.d: 1. To take the stopple or stopper from; as, to unstop a bottle or a cask. 2. To free from any obstruction; to open.

UNSTRAIN.d: To relieve from a strain; to relax. B. Jonson.

m: Not strained; not cleared or purified by straining
UNSTRAINED.d: 1. Not strained; not cleared or purified by straining; as, unstrained oil or milk. 2. Not forced; easy; natural; as, a unstrained deduction or inference. Hakewill.

m: Not stratified; -- applied to massive rocks, as granite, porphyry, etc., and also to deposits of loose material, as the glacial till, which occur in masses without layers or strata.
UNSTRATIFIED.d: Not stratified; -- applied to massive rocks, as granite, porphyry, etc., and also to deposits of loose material, as the glacial till, which occur in masses without layers or strata.

UNSTRENGTH.d: Want of strength; weakness; feebleness. [Obs.] Wyclif.

m: To deprive of a string or strings; also, to take from a string
To loosen the string or strings of
To relax the tension of; to loosen. "His garland they unstring." Dryden. Used also figuratively
e: to unstring a harp or a bow
UNSTRING.d: 1. To deprive of a string or strings; also, to take from a string; as, to unstring beads. 2. To loosen the string or strings of; as, to unstring a harp or a bow. 3. To relax the tension of; to loosen. "His garland they unstring." Dryden.  Used also figuratively; as, his nerves were unstrung by fear.

m: (Nat. Hist.) Without marks or striations; nonstriated
UNSTRIPED.d: 1. Not striped. 2. (Nat. Hist.)  Without marks or striations; nonstriated; as, unstriped muscle fibers.

m: Not studied; not acquired by study; unlabored; natural.
Not skilled; unversed; -- followed by in.
Not spent in study. [Obs.] "To cloak the defects of their unstudied years." Milton.
e: To cloak the defects of their unstudied years.
UNSTUDIED.d: 1. Not studied; not acquired by study; unlabored; natural. 2. Not skilled; unversed; -- followed by in. 3. Not spent in study. [Obs.] "To cloak the defects of their unstudied years." Milton.

UNSUBSTANTIAL.d: Lacking in matter or substance; visionary; chimerical.

m: Not able or likely to succeed. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.
UNSUCCEEDABLE.d: Not able or likely to succeed. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

UNSUCCESS.d: Want of success; failure; misfortune. Prof. Wilson.

m: meeting with, or resulting in, failure
UNSUCCESSFUL.d: Not successful; not producing the desired event; not fortunate; meeting with, or resulting in, failure; unlucky; unhappy. -- Un`suc*cess"ful*ly, adv. -- Un`suc*cess"ful*ness, n.

m: Inability or incapability of enduring, or of being endured. [Obs.] Wyclif.
UNSUFFERING.d: Inability or incapability of enduring, or of being endured. [Obs.] Wyclif.

UNSUIT.d: Not to suit; to be unfit for. [Obs.] Quarles.

m: unendurable. -- Un`sup*port"a*ble*ness, n. Bp. Wilkins. -- Un`sup*port"a*bly, adv.
UNSUPPORTABLE.d: Insupportable; unendurable. -- Un`sup*port"a*ble*ness, n. Bp. Wilkins. -- Un`sup*port"a*bly, adv.

m: Not made sure. [Obs.] Thy now unsured assurance to the crown. Shak.
UNSURED.d: Not made sure. [Obs.] Thy now unsured assurance to the crown. Shak.

UNSURETY.d: Want of surety; uncertainty; insecurity; doubt. [Obs.] Sir T. More.

m: The quality or state of being unsuspecting. Dickens.
UNSUSPICION.d: The quality or state of being unsuspecting. Dickens.

UNSWADDLE.d: To take a swaddle from; to unswathe.

UNSWATHE.d: To take a swathe from; to relieve from a bandage; to unswaddle. Addison.

m: Not capable of being swayed. Shak.
UNSWAYABLE.d: Not capable of being swayed. Shak.

m: To recant or recall, as an oath
to abjure. J. Fletcher. To recall an oath. Spenser.
UNSWEAR.d: To recant or recall, as an oath; to recall after having sworn; to abjure. J. Fletcher.  To recall an oath. Spenser.

m: to ease or cool after exercise or toil. [R.] Milton.
UNSWEAT.d: To relieve from perspiration; to ease or cool after exercise or toil. [R.] Milton.

m: To sink from a swollen state
UNSWELL.d: To sink from a swollen state; to subside. [Obs.] Chaucer.

m: Wanting in symmetry, or due proportion pf parts.
(Biol.) Not symmetrical; being without symmetry, as the parts of a flower when similar parts are of different size and shape, or when the parts of successive circles differ in number. See Symmetry.

(Chem.) Being without symmetry of chemical structure or relation Unsymmetrical carbon atom (Chem.), one which is united at once to four different atoms or radicals. This condition usually occasions physical isomerism, with the attendant action on polarized light.
UNSYMMETRICAL.d: 1. Wanting in symmetry, or due proportion pf parts. 2. (Biol.)  Not symmetrical; being without symmetry, as the parts of a flower when similar parts are of different size and shape, or when the parts of successive circles differ in number. See Symmetry. 3. (Chem.)  Being without symmetry of chemical structure or relation; as, an unsymmetrical carbon atom. Unsymmetrical carbon atom (Chem.), one which is united at once to four different atoms or radicals. This condition usually occasions physical isomerism, with the attendant action on polarized light.

m: To separate, as what is tacked
to release. being untacked from honest cares. Barrow.
UNTACK.d: To separate, as what is tacked; to disjoin; to release. being untacked from honest cares. Barrow.

m: not mentioned; -- often with of. Shak.
UNTALKED.d: Not talked; not mentioned; -- often with of. Shak.

m: To loose from tangles or intricacy
as, to untangle thread. Untangle but this cruel chain. Prior.
UNTANGLE.d: To loose from tangles or intricacy; to disentangle; to resolve; as, to untangle thread. Untangle but this cruel chain. Prior.

m: to come out of concealment. [Obs.] Massinger.
UNTAPPICE.d: to come out of concealment. [Obs.] Massinger.

m: To deprive of a taste for a thing. [R.] Daniel.
UNTASTE.d: To deprive of a taste for a thing. [R.] Daniel.

m: To cause to forget, or to lose from memory, or to disbelieve what has been taught. Experience will unteach us. Sir T. Browne. One breast laid open were a school Which would unteach mankind the lust to shine or rule. Byron.
To cause to be forgotten Dryden.
e: to unteach what has been learned
UNTEACH.d: 1. To cause to forget, or to lose from memory, or to disbelieve what has been taught. Experience will unteach us. Sir T. Browne. One breast laid open were a school Which would unteach mankind the lust to shine or rule. Byron. 2. To cause to be forgotten; as, to unteach what has been learned. Dryden.

m: To unyoke a team from. [R.] Jer. Taylor.
UNTEAM.d: To unyoke a team from. [R.] Jer. Taylor.

m: To deprive of temper, or of the proper degree of temper
UNTEMPER.d: To deprive of temper, or of the proper degree of temper; to make soft.

m: One who does not tempt, or is not a tempter. [Obs.] Wyclif.
UNTEMPTER.d: One who does not tempt, or is not a tempter. [Obs.] Wyclif.

m: To remove a tenant from. [R.] Coleridge.
UNTENANT.d: To remove a tenant from. [R.] Coleridge.

m: To bring out of a tent. [R.] Shak.
UNTENT.d: To bring out of a tent. [R.] Shak.

m: Having no tent or tents, as a soldier or a field. Not tended
not dressed. See 4th Tent. The untented woundings of a father's curse Pierce every sense about thee! Shak.
UNTENTED.d: Having no tent or tents, as a soldier or a field.  Not tended; not dressed. See 4th Tent. The untented woundings of a father's curse Pierce every sense about thee! Shak.

m: misfortune. [Obs.] Unthank come on his head that bound him so. Chaucer.
UNTHANK.d: No thanks; ill will; misfortune. [Obs.] Unthank come on his head that bound him so. Chaucer.

m: To recall or take back, as something thought. Shak.
UNTHINK.d: To recall or take back, as something thought. Shak.

m: A person who does not think, or does not think wisely.
UNTHINKER.d: A person who does not think, or does not think wisely.

m: Not thinking; not heedful; thoughtless; inconsiderate
Not indicating thought or reflection; thoughtless. With earnest eyes, and round unthinking face, He first the snuffbox opened, then the case. Pope. -- Un*think"ing*ly, adv. -- Un*think"ing*ness, n.
UNTHINKING.d: 1. Not thinking; not heedful; thoughtless; inconsiderate; as, unthinking youth. 2. Not indicating thought or reflection; thoughtless. With earnest eyes, and round unthinking face, He first the snuffbox opened, then the case. Pope. -- Un*think"ing*ly, adv. -- Un*think"ing*ness, n.

m: To draw or take out a thread from
To deprive of ligaments; to loose the ligaments of. He with his bare wand can unthread thy joints. Milton.
To make one's way through; to traverse De Quincey.
UNTHREAD.d: 1. To draw or take out a thread from; as, to unthread a needle. 2. To deprive of ligaments; to loose the ligaments of. He with his bare wand can unthread thy joints. Milton. 3. To make one's way through; to traverse; as, to unthread a devious path. De Quincey.

UNTHRIFT.d: 1. Want of thrift; untriftiness; prodigality. 2. An unthrifty. [Obs.] Dryden.  Unthrifty. [Obs.]

m: Not thriftily. [Obs.] "Unthriftfully spent." Sir J. Cheke.
UNTHRIFTFULLY.d: Not thriftily. [Obs.] "Unthriftfully spent." Sir J. Cheke.

m: The quality or state or being unthrifty
UNTHRIFTINESS.d: The quality or state or being unthrifty; profuseness; lavishness. Udall.

m: To remove from, or as from, a throne
UNTHRONE.d: To remove from, or as from, a throne; to dethrone. Milton.

m: Not tidy or neat; slovenly. -- Un*ti"di*ly, adv. -- Un*ti"di*ness, n.
UNTIDY.d: 1. Unseasonable; untimely. [Obs.] "Untidy tales." Piers Plowman. 2. Not tidy or neat; slovenly. -- Un*ti"di*ly, adv. -- Un*ti"di*ness, n.

m: To loosen, as something interlaced or knotted; to disengage the parts of Sacharissa's captive fain Would untie his iron chain. Waller. Her snakes untied, sulphurous waters drink. Pope.

To free from fastening or from restraint; to let loose; to unbind. Though you untie the winds, and let them fight Against the churches. Shak. All the evils of an untied tongue we put upon the accounts of drunkenness. Jer. Taylor.
To resolve; to unfold; to clear. They quicken sloth, perplexities untie. Denham. To become untied or loosed.
UNTIE.d: 1. To loosen, as something interlaced or knotted; to disengage the parts of; as, to untie a knot. Sacharissa's captive fain Would untie his iron chain. Waller. Her snakes untied, sulphurous waters drink. Pope. 2. To free from fastening or from restraint; to let loose; to unbind. Though you untie the winds, and let them fight Against the churches. Shak. All the evils of an untied tongue we put upon the accounts of drunkenness. Jer. Taylor. 3. To resolve; to unfold; to clear. They quicken sloth, perplexities untie. Denham.  To become untied or loosed.

m: To make less tight or tense
UNTIGHTEN.d: To make less tight or tense; to loosen.

m: To; unto; towards; -- used of material objects. Chaucer. Taverners until them told the same. Piers Plowman. He roused himself full blithe, and hastened them until. Spenser.
To; up to; till; before; -- used of time he will not come back until the end of the month. He and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity. Judg. xviii.

Note: In contracts and like documents until is construed as exclusive of the date mentioned unless it was the manifest intent of the parties to include it. As far as; to the place or degree that; especially, up to the time that; till. See Till, conj. In open prospect nothing bounds our eye, Until the earth seems joined unto the sky. Dryden. But the rest of the dead lives not again until the thousand years were finished. Rev. xx. 5.
UNTIL.d: 1. To; unto; towards; -- used of material objects. Chaucer. Taverners until them told the same. Piers Plowman. He roused himself full blithe, and hastened them until. Spenser. 2. To; up to; till; before; -- used of time; as, he staid until evening; he will not come back until the end of the month. He and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity. Judg. xviii. 30. Note: In contracts and like documents until is construed as exclusive of the date mentioned unless it was the manifest intent of the parties to include it.  As far as; to the place or degree that; especially, up to the time that; till. See Till, conj. In open prospect nothing bounds our eye, Until the earth seems joined unto the sky. Dryden. But the rest of the dead lives not again until the thousand years were finished. Rev. xx. 5.

m: to uncover by removing the tiles.
UNTILE.d: To take the tiles from; to uncover by removing the tiles.

m: An unseasonable time. [Obs.] A man shall not eat in untime. Chaucer.
UNTIME.d: An unseasonable time. [Obs.] A man shall not eat in untime. Chaucer.

m: done or happening at an unnatural, unusual, or improper time
UNTIMELY.d: Not timely; done or happening at an unnatural, unusual, or improper time; unseasonable; premature; inopportune; as, untimely frosts; untimely remarks; an untimely death.  Out of the natural or usual time; inopportunely; prematurely; unseasonably. "Let them know . . . what's untimely done." Shak.

m: Not titled; having no title, or appellation of dignity or distinction. Spenser.
Being without title or right; not entitled. Shak.
UNTITLED.d: 1. Not titled; having no title, or appellation of dignity or distinction. Spenser. 2. Being without title or right; not entitled. Shak.

m: To; -- now used only in antiquated, formal, or scriptural style. See To.
Until; till. [Obs.] "He shall abide it unto the death of the priest." Num. xxxv.
Until; till. [Obs.] "Unto this year be gone." Chaucer.
e: He shall abide it unto the death of the priest.
UNTO.d: 1. To; -- now used only in antiquated, formal, or scriptural style. See To. 2. Until; till. [Obs.] "He shall abide it unto the death of the priest." Num. xxxv. 25.  Until; till. [Obs.] "Unto this year be gone." Chaucer.

m: Not told; not related; not revealed
UNTOLD.d: 1. Not told; not related; not revealed; as, untold secrets. 2. Not numbered or counted; as, untold money.

UNTOMB.d: To take from the tomb; to exhume; to disinter. Fuller.

m: To deprive of a tongue, or of voice. [Obs.] Fuller.
UNTONGUE.d: To deprive of a tongue, or of voice. [Obs.] Fuller.

m: To take out the teeth of. Cowper.
UNTOOTH.d: To take out the teeth of. Cowper.

m: Froward; perverse. "Save yourselves from this untoward generation." Acts ii.
2. Awkward; ungraceful. "Untoward words." Creech. "Untoward manner." Swift.
Inconvenient; troublesome; vexatious; unlucky; unfortunate -- Un*to"ward*ly, adv. -- Un*to"ward*ness, n.
e: Save yourselves from this untoward generation.
UNTOWARD.d: Toward. [Obs.] Gower.  1. Froward; perverse. "Save yourselves from this untoward generation." Acts ii. 40. 2. Awkward; ungraceful. "Untoward words." Creech. "Untoward manner." Swift. 3. Inconvenient; troublesome; vexatious; unlucky; unfortunate; as, an untoward wind or accident. -- Un*to"ward*ly, adv. -- Un*to"ward*ness, n.

UNTOWARDLY.d: Perverse; froward; untoward. "Untowardly tricks and vices." Locke.

m: Not dealt with in trade; not visited for purposes of trade. [Obs.] Hakluyt
Not traded in or bartered; hence, not hackneyed; unusual; not common. Shak.
UNTRADED.d: 1. Not dealt with in trade; not visited for purposes of trade. [Obs.] Hakluyt 2. Unpracticed; inexperienced. [Obs.] Udall. 3. Not traded in or bartered; hence, not hackneyed; unusual; not common. Shak.

UNTRAINED.d: 1. Not trained. Shak. 2. Not trainable; indocile. [Obs.] Herbert.

UNTRAMMELED.d: Not hampered or impeded; free. [Written also untrammelled.]

m: Not traveled; not trodden by passengers
Having never visited foreign countries; not having gained knowledge or experience by travel Addison.
UNTRAVELED.d: 1. Not traveled; not trodden by passengers; as, an untraveled forest. 2. Having never visited foreign countries; not having gained knowledge or experience by travel; as, an untraveled Englishman. Addison.

UNTREAD.d: To tread back; to retrace. Shak.

m: To bring forth or give up, as things previously treasured. "The quaintness with which he untreasured, as by rote, the stores of his memory." J. Mitford.
UNTREASURE.d: To bring forth or give up, as things previously treasured. "The quaintness with which he untreasured, as by rote, the stores of his memory." J. Mitford.

m: Etym: [Properly p. p. of untreasure.] Deprived of treasure. [Obs.] Shak.
Etym: [Pref. un- not + treasured.] Not treasured; not kept as treasure.
UNTREASURED.d: 1. Etym: [Properly p. p. of untreasure.]  Deprived of treasure. [Obs.] Shak. 2. Etym: [Pref. un- not + treasured.]  Not treasured; not kept as treasure.

UNTREATABLE.d: Incapable of being treated; not practicable. [R.] Dr. H. More.

m: unarranged; -- said of the hair. Chaucer.
UNTRESSED.d: Not tied up in tresses; unarranged; -- said of the hair. Chaucer.

m: Not true; false; contrary to the fact
Not faithful; inconstant; false; disloyal. Chaucer. Untruly. [Obs. or Poetic] Chaucer.
UNTRUE.d: 1. Not true; false; contrary to the fact; as, the story is untrue. 2. Not faithful; inconstant; false; disloyal. Chaucer.  Untruly. [Obs. or Poetic] Chaucer.

m: a false statement. [Recent & R.] A. Trollope.
UNTRUISM.d: Something not true; a false statement. [Recent & R.] A. Trollope.

m: Separated from its trunk or stock. [Obs.]
UNTRUNKED.d: Separated from its trunk or stock. [Obs.]

m: To loose from a truss, or as from a truss
to undress. [R.] Dryden. One who untrussed persons for the purpose of flogging them
UNTRUSS.d: To loose from a truss, or as from a truss; to untie or unfasten; to let out; to undress. [R.] Dryden.  One who untrussed persons for the purpose of flogging them; a public whipper. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

m: One who untrussed persons for the purpose of flogging them
UNTRUSSER.d: One who untrussed persons for the purpose of flogging them; a public whipper. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

m: Not to be trusted; not trusty. [R.] Sir W. Scott.
UNTRUSTFUL.d: 1. Not trustful or trusting. 2. Not to be trusted; not trusty. [R.] Sir W. Scott.

m: The quality of being untrue; contrariety to truth; want of veracity; also, treachery; faithlessness; disloyalty. Chaucer.
That which is untrue; a false assertion; a falsehood; a lie; also, an act of treachery or disloyalty. Shak. Syn. -- Lie; falsehood. See Lie.
UNTRUTH.d: 1. The quality of being untrue; contrariety to truth; want of veracity; also, treachery; faithlessness; disloyalty. Chaucer. 2. That which is untrue; a false assertion; a falsehood; a lie; also, an act of treachery or disloyalty. Shak. Syn. -- Lie; falsehood. See Lie.

m: contrary to the truth or the fact. -- Un*truth"ful*ly, adv. -- Un*truth"ful*ness, n.
UNTRUTHFUL.d: Not truthful; unveracious; contrary to the truth or the fact. -- Un*truth"ful*ly, adv. -- Un*truth"ful*ness, n.

m: To unfold or undo, as a tuck
to release from a tuck or fold.
UNTUCK.d: To unfold or undo, as a tuck; to release from a tuck or fold.

m: To make incapable of harmony, or of harmonious action
to put out of tune. Shak.
UNTUNE.d: To make incapable of harmony, or of harmonious action; to put out of tune. Shak.

m: To turn in a reserve way, especially so as to open something
as, to unturn a key. Keats.
UNTURN.d: To turn in a reserve way, especially so as to open something; as, to unturn a key. Keats.

m: not revolved or reversed. To leave no stone unturned, to leave nothing untried for accomplishing one's purpose. [He] left unturned no stone To make my guilt appear, and hide his own. Dryden.
UNTURNED.d: Not turned; not revolved or reversed. To leave no stone unturned, to leave nothing untried for accomplishing one's purpose. [He] left unturned no stone To make my guilt appear, and hide his own. Dryden.

UNTWAIN.d: To rend in twain; to tear in two. [Obs.] Skelton.

m: to separate, as that which is twined or twisted
to untie. It requires a long and powerful counter sympathy in a nation to untwine the ties of custom which bind a people to the established and the old. Sir W. Hamilton. To become untwined. Milton.
UNTWINE.d: To untwist; to separate, as that which is twined or twisted; to disentangle; to untie. It requires a long and powerful counter sympathy in a nation to untwine the ties of custom which bind a people to the established and the old. Sir W. Hamilton.  To become untwined. Milton.

m: Aloft; on high; in a direction contrary to that of gravity; toward or in a higher place or position; above; -- the opposite of Ant: down. But up or down, By center or eccentric, hard to tell. Milton.

Hence, in many derived uses, specifically: -- (a) From a lower to a higher position, literally or figuratively from the mouth, toward the source, of a river; from a dependent or inferior condition; from concealment; from younger age; from a quiet state, or the like; -- used with verbs of motion expressed or implied. But they presumed to go up unto the hilltop. Num. xiv.
I am afflicted and ready to die from my youth up. Ps. lxxxviii.

Up rose the sun, and up rose Emelye. Chaucer. We have wrought ourselves up into this degree of Christian indifference. Atterbury. (b) In a higher place or position, literally or figuratively; in the state of having arisen; in an upright, or nearly upright, position; standing; mounted on a horse; in a condition of elevation, prominence, advance, proficiency, excitement, insurrection, or the like; -- used with verbs of rest, situation, condition, and the like the lid of the box was up; prices are up. And when the sun was up, they were scorched. Matt. xiii.
e: from a recumbent or sitting position
to be up on a hill
UP.d: 1. Aloft; on high; in a direction contrary to that of gravity; toward or in a higher place or position; above; -- the opposite of Ant: down. But up or down, By center or eccentric, hard to tell. Milton. 2. Hence, in many derived uses, specifically: -- (a) From a lower to a higher position, literally or figuratively; as, from a recumbent or sitting position; from the mouth, toward the source, of a river; from a dependent or inferior condition; from concealment; from younger age; from a quiet state, or the like; -- used with verbs of motion expressed or implied. But they presumed to go up unto the hilltop. Num. xiv. 44. I am afflicted and ready to die from my youth up. Ps. lxxxviii. 15. Up rose the sun, and up rose Emelye. Chaucer. We have wrought ourselves up into this degree of Christian indifference. Atterbury. (b) In a higher place or position, literally or figuratively; in the state of having arisen; in an upright, or nearly upright, position; standing; mounted on a horse; in a condition of elevation, prominence, advance, proficiency, excitement, insurrection, or the like; -- used with verbs of rest, situation, condition, and the like; as, to be up on a hill; the lid of the box was up; prices are up. And when the sun was up, they were scorched. Matt. xiii. 6. Those that were up themselves kept others low. Spenser. Helen was up -- was she Shak. Rebels there are up, And put the Englishmen unto the sword. Shak. His name was up through all the adjoining provinces, even to Italy and Rome; many desiring to see who he was that could withstand so many years the Roman puissance. Milton. Thou hast fired me; my soul's up in arms. Dryden. Grief and passion are like floods raised in little brooks by a sudden rain; they are quickly up. Dryden. A general whisper ran among the country people, that Sir Roger was up. Addison. Let us, then, be up and doing, With a heart for any fate. Longfellow. (c) To or in a position of equal advance or equality; not short of, back of, less advanced than, away from, or the like; -- usually followed by to or with; as, to be up to the chin in water; to come up with one's companions; to come up with the enemy; to live up to engagements. As a boar was whetting his teeth, up comes a fox to him. L'Estrange. (d) To or in a state of completion; completely; wholly; quite; as, in the phrases to eat up; to drink up; to burn up; to sum up; etc.; to shut up the eyes or the mouth; to sew up a rent. Note: Some phrases of this kind are now obsolete; as, to spend up (Prov. xxi. 20); to kill up (B. Jonson). (e) Aside, so as not to be in use; as, to lay up riches; put up your weapons. Note: Up is used elliptically for get up, rouse up, etc., expressing a command or exhortation. "Up, and let us be going." Judg. xix. 28. Up, up, my friend! and quit your books, Or surely you 'll grow double. Wordsworth. It is all up with him, it is all over with him; he is lost. -- The time is up, the allotted time is past. -- To be up in, to be informed about; to be versed in. "Anxious that their sons should be well up in the superstitions of two thousand years ago." H. Spencer. -- To be up to. (a) To be equal to, or prepared for; as, he is up to the business, or the emergency. [Colloq.] (b) To be engaged in; to purpose, with the idea of doing ill or mischief; as, I don't know what he's up to. [Colloq.] -- To blow up. (a) To inflate; to distend. (b) To destroy by an explosion from beneath. (c) To explode; as, the boiler blew up. (d) To reprove angrily; to scold. [Slang] -- To bring up. See under Bring, v. t. -- To come up with. See under Come, v. i. -- To cut up. See under Cut, v. t. & i. -- To draw up. See under Draw, v. t. -- To grow up, to grow to maturity. -- Up anchor (Naut.), the order to man the windlass preparatory to hauling up the anchor. -- Up and down. (a) First up, and then down; from one state or position to another. See under Down, adv. Fortune . . . led him up and down. Chaucer. (b) (Naut.) Vertical; perpendicular; -- said of the cable when the anchor is under, or nearly under, the hawse hole, and the cable is taut. Totten. -- Up helm (Naut.), the order given to move the tiller toward the upper, or windward, side of a vessel. -- Up to snuff. See under Snuff. [Slang] -- What is up What is going on [Slang]  1. From a lower to a higher place on, upon, or along; at a higher situation upon; at the top of. In going up a hill, the knees will be most weary; in going down, the thihgs. Bacon. 2. From the coast towards the interior of, as a country; from the mouth towards the source of, as a stream; as, to journey up the country; to sail up the Hudson. 3. Upon. [Obs.] "Up pain of death." Chaucer.  The state of being up or above; a state of elevation, prosperity, or the like; -- rarely occurring except in the phrase ups and downs. [Colloq.] Ups and downs, alternate states of elevation and depression, or of prosperity and the contrary. [Colloq.] They had their ups and downs of fortune. Thackeray.  Inclining up; tending or going up; upward; as, an up look; an up grade; the up train.

m: The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. Judg. xvi.

As I did stand my watch upon the hill. Shak. He made a great difference between people that did rebel upon wantonness, and them that did rebel upon want. Bacon. This advantage we lost upon the invention of firearms. Addison. Upon the whole, it will be necessary to avoid that perpetual repetition of the same epithets which we find in Homer. Pope. He had abandoned the frontiers, retiring upon Glasgow. Sir. W. Scott. Philip swore upon the Evangelists to abstain from aggression in my absence. Landor. Note: Upon conveys a more distinct notion that on carries with it of something that literally or metaphorically bears or supports. It is less employed than it used to be, on having for the most part taken its place. Some expressions formed with it belong only to old style that is, in consequence of pity: upon the rate of thirty thousand; that is, amounting to the rate: to die upon the hand; that is, by means of the hand: he had a garment upon; that is, upon himself: the time is coming fast upon; that is, upon the present time. By the omission of its object, upon acquires an adverbial sense, as in the last two examples. To assure upon (Law), to promise; to undertake. -- To come upon. See under Come. -- To take upon, to assume.
e: upon pity they were taken away
UPON.d: On; -- used in all the senses of that word, with which it is interchangeable. "Upon an hill of flowers." Chaucer. Our host upon his stirrups stood anon. Chaucer. Thou shalt take of the blood that is upon the altar. Ex. xxix. 21. The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. Judg. xvi. 9. As I did stand my watch upon the hill. Shak. He made a great difference between people that did rebel upon wantonness, and them that did rebel upon want. Bacon. This advantage we lost upon the invention of firearms. Addison. Upon the whole, it will be necessary to avoid that perpetual repetition of the same epithets which we find in Homer. Pope. He had abandoned the frontiers, retiring upon Glasgow. Sir. W. Scott. Philip swore upon the Evangelists to abstain from aggression in my absence. Landor. Note: Upon conveys a more distinct notion that on carries with it of something that literally or metaphorically bears or supports. It is less employed than it used to be, on having for the most part taken its place. m: A very soluble crystalline body which is the chief constituent of the urine in mammals and some other animals. It is also present in small quantity in blood, serous fluids, lymph, the liver, etc. Note: It is the main product of the regressive metamorphosis (katabolism) of proteid matter in the body, and is excreted daily to the amount of about 500 grains by a man of average weight. Chemically it is carbamide, CO(NH2)2, and when heated with strong acids or alkalies is decomposed into carbonic acid and ammonia. It unites with acids to form salts, as nitrate of urea, and it can be made synthetically from ammonium cyanate, with which it is isomeric. Urea ferment, a soluble ferment formed by certain bacteria, which, however, yield the ferment from the body of their cells only after they have been killed by alcohol. It causes urea to take up water and decompose into carbonic acid and ammonia. Many different bacteria possess this property, especially Bacterium ureæ and Micrococcus ureæ, which are found abundantly in urines undergoing alkaline fermentation.
UREA.d: A very soluble crystalline body which is the chief constituent of the urine in mammals and some other animals. Chemically it is carbamide, CO(NH2)2, and when heated with strong acids or alkalies is decomposed into carbonic acid and ammonia. Combined in the form of urate of ammonia, it is the chief constituent of the urine of birds and reptiles, forming the white part. Traces of it are also found in the various organs of the body. It is likewise a common constituent, either as the free acid or as a urate, of urinary or renal calculi and of the so-called gouty concretions. From acid urines, uric acid is frequently deposited, on standing in a cool place, in the form of a reddish yellow sediment, nearly always crystalline. Chemically, it is composed of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen, C5H4N4O3, and by decomposition yields urea, among other products. It can be made synthetically by heating together urea and glycocoll. It was formerly called also lithic acid, in allusion to its occurrence in stone, or calculus.

m: In mammals, a fluid excretion from the kidneys

in birds and reptiles, a solid or semisolid excretion. Note: In man, the urine is a clear, transparent fluid of an amber color and peculiar odor, with an average density of 1.02. The average amount excreted in 24 hours is from 40 to 60 ounces (about 1,200 cubic centimeters). Chemically, the urine is mainly an aqueous solution of urea, salt (sodium chloride), and uric acid, together with some hippuric acid and peculiar pigments. It usually has an acid reaction, owing to the presence of acid phosphates of soda or free uric acid. Normally, it contains about 960 parts of water to 40 parts of solid matter, and the daily average excretion is 35 grams (540 grains) of urea, 0.75 gram (11 grains) of uric acid, and 16.5 grams (260 grains) of salt. Abnormally, it may contain sugar as in diabetes, albumen as in Bright's disease, bile pigments as in jaundice, or abnormal quantities of some one or more of the normal constituents. To urinate. [Obs.] Bacon.

USAGE.d: 1. The act of using; mode of using or treating; treatment; conduct with respect to a person or a thing; as, good usage; ill usage; hard usage. My brother Is prisoner to the bishop here, at whose hands He hath good usage and great liberty. Shak. 2. Manners; conduct; behavior. [Obs.] A gentle nymph was found, Hight Astery, excelling all the crew In courteous usage. Spenser. 3. Long-continued practice; customary mode of procedure; custom; habitual use; method. Chaucer. It has now been, during many years, the grave and decorous usage of Parliaments to hear, in respectful silence, all expressions, acceptable or unacceptable, which are uttered from the throne. Macaulay. 4. Customary use or employment, as of a word or phrase in a particular sense or signification. 5. Experience. [Obs.] In eld [old age] is both wisdom and usage. Chaucer. Syn. -- Custom; use; habit. -- Usage, Custom. These words, as here compared, agree in expressing the idea of habitual practice; but a custom is not necessarily a usage. A custom may belong to many, or to a single individual. A usage properly belongs to the great body of a people. Hence, we speak of usage, not of custom, as the law of language. Again, a custom is merely that which has been often repeated, so as to have become, in a good degree, established. A usage must be both often repeated and of long standing. Hence, we speak of a "hew custom," but not of a "new usage." Thus, also, the "customs of society" is not so strong an expression as the "usages of society." "Custom, a greater power than nature, seldom fails to make them worship." Locke. "Of things once received and confirmed by use, long usage is a law sufficient." Hooker. In law, the words usage and custom are often used interchangeably, but the word custom also has a technical and restricted sense. See Custom, n., 3.

to have no further use for a book
USE.d: 1. The act of employing anything, or of applying it to one's service; the state of being so employed or applied; application; employment; conversion to some purpose; as, the use of a pen in writing; his machines are in general use. Books can never teach the use of books. Bacon. This Davy serves you for good uses. Shak. When he framed All things to man's delightful use. Milton. 2. Occasion or need to employ; necessity; as, to have no further use for a book. Shak. 3. Yielding of service; advantage derived; capability of being used; usefulness; utility. God made two great lights, great for their use To man. Milton. 'T is use alone that sanctifies expense. Pope. 4. Continued or repeated practice; customary employment; usage; custom; manner; habit. Let later age that noble use envy. Spenser. How weary, stale, flat and unprofitable, Seem to me all the uses of this world! Shak. 5. Common occurrence; ordinary experience. [R.] O Cæsar! these things are beyond all use. Shak. 6. (Eccl.)  The special form of ritual adopted for use in any diocese; as, the Sarum, or Canterbury, use; the Hereford use; the York use; the Roman use; etc. From henceforth all the whole realm shall have but one use. Pref. to Book of Common Prayer. 7. The premium paid for the possession and employment of borrowed money; interest; usury. [Obs.] Thou art more obliged to pay duty and tribute, use and principal, to him. Jer. Taylor. 8. Etym: [In this sense probably a corruption of OF. oes, fr. L. opus need, business, employment, work. Cf. Operate.] (Law)  The benefit or profit of lands and tenements. Use imports a trust and confidence reposed in a man for the holding of lands. He to whose use or benefit the trust is intended shall enjoy the profits. An estate is granted and limited to A for the use of B. 9. (Forging)  A stab of iron welded to the side of a forging, as a shaft, near the end, and afterward drawn down, by hammering, so as to lengthen the forging. Contingent, or Springing, use (Law), a use to come into operation on a future uncertain event. -- In use. (a) In employment; in customary practice observance. (b) In heat; -- said especially of mares. J. H. Walsh. -- Of no use, useless; of no advantage. -- Of use, useful; of advantage; profitable. -- Out of use, not in employment. -- Resulting use (Law), a use, which, being limited by the deed, expires or can not vest, and results or returns to him who raised it, after such expiration. -- Secondary, or Shifting, use, a use which, though executed, may change from one to another by circumstances. Blackstone. -- Statute of uses (Eng. Law), the stat. 27 Henry VIII., cap. 10, which transfers uses into possession, or which unites the use and possession. -- To make use of, To put to use, to employ; to derive service from; to use.  1. To make use of; to convert to one's service; to avail one's self of; to employ; to put a purpose; as, to use a plow; to use a chair; to use time; to use flour for food; to use water for irrigation. Launcelot Gobbo, use your legs. Shak. Some other means I have which may be used. Milton. 2. To behave toward; to act with regard to; to treat; as, to use a beast cruelly. "I will use him well." Shak. How wouldst thou use me now Milton. Cato has used me ill. Addison. 3. To practice customarily; to make a practice of; as, to use diligence in business. Use hospitality one to another. 1 Pet. iv. 9. 4. To accustom; to habituate; to render familiar by practice; to inure; -- employed chiefly in the passive participle; as, men used to cold and hunger; soldiers used to hardships and danger. I am so used in the fire to blow. Chaucer. Thou with thy compeers, Used to the yoke, draw'st his triumphant wheels. Milton. To use one's self, to behave. [Obs.] "Pray, forgive me, if I have used myself unmannerly." Shak. -- To use up. (a) To consume or exhaust by using; to leave nothing of; as, to use up the supplies. (b) To exhaust; to tire out; to leave no capacity of force or use in; to overthrow; as, he was used up by fatigue. [Colloq.] Syn. -- Employ. -- Use, Employ. We use a thing, or make use of it, when we derive from it some enjoyment or service. We employ it when we turn that service into a particular channel. We use words to express our general meaning; we employ certain technical terms in reference to a given subject. To make use of, implies passivity in the thing; as, to make use of a pen; and hence there is often a material difference between the two words when applied to persons. To speak of "making use of another" generally implies a degrading idea, as if we had used him as a tool; while employ has no such sense. A confidential friend is employed to negotiate; an inferior agent is made use of on an intrigue. I would, my son, that thou wouldst use the power Which thy discretion gives thee, to control And manage all. Cowper. To study nature will thy time employ: Knowledge and innocence are perfect joy. Dryden.  1. To be wont or accustomed; to be in the habit or practice; as, he used to ride daily; -- now disused in the present tense, perhaps because of the similarity in sound, between "use to," and "used to." They use to place him that shall be their captain on a stone. Spenser. Fears use to be represented in an imaginary. Bacon. Thus we use to say, it is the room that smokes, when indeed it is the fire in the room. South. Now Moses used to take the tent and to pitch it without the camp. Ex. xxxiii. 7 (Rev. Ver.) 2. To be accustomed to go; to frequent; to inhabit; to dwell; -- sometimes followed by of. [Obs.] "Where never foot did use." Spenser. He useth every day to a merchant's house. B. Jonson. Ye valleys low, where the mild whispers use Of shades, and wanton winds, and gushing brooks. Milton.

USEFUL.d: Full of use, advantage, or profit; producing, or having power to produce, good; serviceable for any end or object; helpful toward advancing any purpose; beneficial; profitable; advantageous; as, vessels and instruments useful in a family; books useful for improvement; useful knowledge; useful arts. USEFULNESS.d: The quality or state of being useful; utility; serviceableness; advantage. Addison. Syn. -- Utility; value; profit. See Utility.

m: Having, or being of, no use
USELESS.d: Having, or being of, no use; unserviceable; producing no good end; answering no valuable purpose; not advancing the end proposed; unprofitable; ineffectual; as, a useless garment; useless pity. Not to sit idle with so great a gift Useless, and thence ridiculous. Milton. Syn. -- Fruitless; ineffectual. -- Useless, Fruitless, Ineffectual. We speak of an attempt, effort, etc., as being useless when there are in it inherent difficulties which forbid the hope of success, as fruitless when it fails, not from any such difficulties, but from some unexpected hindrance arising to frustrate it; as, the design was rendered fruitless by the death of its projector. Ineffectual nearly resembles fruitless, but implies a failure of a less hopeless character; as, after several ineffectual efforts, I at last succeeded. Useless are all words Till you have writ "performance" with your swords. The other is for waiving. Beau. & Fl. Waiving all searches into antiquity, in relation to this controversy, as being either needless or fruitless. Waterland. Even our blessed Savior's preaching, who spake as never man spake, was ineffectual to many. Bp. Stillingfleet. -- Use"less*ly, adv. -- Use"less*ness, n.

m: To seize, and hold in possession, by force, or without right
to usurp the prerogatives of the crown
USURP.d: To seize, and hold in possession, by force, or without right; as, to usurp a throne; to usurp the prerogatives of the crown; to usurp power; to usurp the right of a patron is to oust or dispossess him. Alack, thou dost usurp authority. Shak. Another revolution, to get rid of this illegitimate and usurped government, would of course be perfectly justifiable. Burke. Note: Usurp is applied to seizure and use of office, functions, powers, rights, etc.; it is not applied to common dispossession of private property. Syn. -- To arrogate; assume; appropriate.  To commit forcible seizure of place, power, functions, or the like, without right; to commit unjust encroachments; to be, or act as, a usurper. The parish churches on which the Presbyterians and fanatics had usurped. Evelyn. And now the Spirits of the Mind Are busy with poor Peter Bell; Upon the rights of visual sense Usurping, with a prevalence More terrible than magic spell. Wordsworth.

Manifest usurpation on the rights of other States. D. Webster. Note: Usurpation, in a peculiar sense, formerly denoted the absolute ouster and dispossession of the patron of a church, by a stranger presenting a clerk to a vacant benefice, who us thereupon admitted and instituted.

m: A premium or increase paid, or stipulated to be paid, for a loan, as of money; interest. [Obs. or Archaic] Thou shalt not lend upon usury to thy brother; usury of money, usury of victuals, usury of anything that is lent upon usury. Deut. xxiii.
Thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchanges, and then at my coming I should have received mine own with usury. Matt. xxv.
What he borrows from the ancients, he repays with usury of Dryden.
The practice of taking interest. [Obs.] Usury . . . bringeth the treasure of a realm or state into a few Bacon.
USURY.d: 1. A premium or increase paid, or stipulated to be paid, for a loan, as of money; interest. [Obs. or Archaic] Thou shalt not lend upon usury to thy brother; usury of money, usury of victuals, usury of anything that is lent upon usury. Deut. xxiii. 19. Thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchanges, and then at my coming I should have received mine own with usury. Matt. xxv. 27. What he borrows from the ancients, he repays with usury of Dryden. 2. The practice of taking interest. [Obs.] Usury . . . bringeth the treasure of a realm or state into a few Bacon. 3. (Law)  Interest in excess of a legal rate charged to a borrower for the use of money. Note: The practice of requiring in repayment of money lent anything more than the amount lent, was formerly thought to be a great moral wrong, and the greater, the more was taken. Now it is not deemed more wrong to take pay for the use of money than for the use of a house, or a horse, or any other property. But the lingering influence of the former opinion, together with the fact that the nature of money makes it easier for the lender to oppress the borrower, has caused nearly all Christian nations to fix by law the rate of compensation for the use of money. Of late years, however, the opinion that money should be borrowed and repaid, or bought and sold, upon whatever terms the parties should agree to, like any other property, has gained ground everywhere. Am. Cyc.
